note: Dante has been walking bent double beside Oderisi, the manuscript painter of Canto 11, keeping pace with him like one of a pair of oxen under a yoke. The yoke is an old image of humility.
He stands up straight, but Oderisi's words about fame and the hint of his own coming exile have humbled him. His thoughts stay bowed.

Each terrace teaches twice: with examples of the virtue to spur the souls on, and examples of the sin punished to rein them in. On this terrace humility was carved on the wall (Canto 10). Pride brought low is carved on the floor, where the bent souls cannot help seeing it.
The stone slabs set into church floors over graves, carved with a likeness of the dead person. Worshippers walk over them, as Dante now walks over these.

Thirteen examples of pride follow, alternating between the Bible and classical myth. In Italian the first four stanzas begin with "Vedea" (I saw), the next four with "O", the next four with "Mostrava" (It showed), and a last stanza uses all three. The initials spell VOM, that is "uom", man: pride is the human sin.

quote: him who was created most noble
context: The first and greatest example of pride. Christ says in the Gospel, "I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven" (Luke 10:18).
Struck down by Jupiter's thunderbolt, the classical match for Lucifer on the other side of the path.

note: Apollo, called by a name taken from his temple at Thymbra, near Troy. Virgil uses the name in the Aeneid.
Pallas is Athena (the Roman Minerva), goddess of wisdom and war. Mars is the god of war.
Jupiter, king of the gods.
The giants piled mountain on mountain to storm the home of the gods, and were destroyed in the battle of Phlegra. Dante sees the survivors chained around the pit of lower Hell in Inferno 31.

context: Shown at the foot of his unfinished tower, staring at workmen who can no longer understand one another.

note: The plain in Mesopotamia where the Tower of Babel was built (Genesis 11:2).

Queen of Thebes in Greek myth. She boasted that her fourteen children made her greater than the goddess Latona, who had only two. Those two, Apollo and Diana, shot all fourteen dead, and Niobe wept until she turned to stone. Ovid tells the story in the Metamorphoses.
The first king of Israel, proud and disobedient to God. Defeated by the Philistines on Mount Gilboa, he fell on his own sword (1 Samuel 31).
David's lament for Saul curses the place: "You mountains of Gilboa, let there be no dew or rain upon you" (2 Samuel 1:21).

A weaver so sure of her skill that she challenged the goddess Minerva to a contest. Minerva could find no flaw in the girl's cloth, tore it to pieces and struck her. Arachne hanged herself, and the goddess turned her into a spider. The story is in Ovid's Metamorphoses.

Son of King Solomon. When the people asked him to lighten their burdens he promised to make them heavier: "My father chastised you with whips, but I will chastise you with scorpions." Ten of the twelve tribes rebelled, and he fled to Jerusalem in his chariot (1 Kings 12).

In Greek myth, he killed his mother, Eriphyle, to avenge his father, Amphiaraus. She had been bribed to reveal where her husband was hiding, so that he had to go to the war against Thebes, where he knew he would die. Dante meets Amphiaraus in Inferno 20.
The bribe: a golden necklace made by the god Vulcan, which brought ruin to every woman who owned it. Eriphyle's vanity counts as her pride.

King of Assyria. Besieging Jerusalem, he mocked the God of Israel as powerless. An angel destroyed his army in one night, and back home his own sons killed him as he prayed in the temple of his god (2 Kings 19).

Queen of the Massagetae, a people of central Asia. Cyrus the Great, founder of the Persian empire, attacked her and caused the death of her son. She destroyed his army and killed him, about 530 BC, and had his head plunged into a skin full of blood, with the words Dante gives her. The story comes from the Greek historian Herodotus, by way of later Latin writers.
The Assyrian general in the biblical Book of Judith. While he besieged a Jewish town, the widow Judith came to his tent, waited until he was drunk and cut off his head. His army fled at the sight.
Probably the headless body of Holofernes, left in his tent.
The last example is a whole city. In the Aeneid Virgil calls it "proud Ilium". In Italian this stanza gathers up the pattern of the others: its three lines begin "I saw", "O" and "It showed".
No human artist made these carvings. Like the reliefs on the wall in Canto 10, they are God's own work, more lifelike than any art.
Dante is still stooping to look. He treads on the images of the proud, as the dead in a church floor are trodden on.
Bitter irony, aimed at the reader. Eve was the first human to sin through pride, wanting to be like God.
The angel of humility. An angel waits at the way up from each terrace, removes the mark of that terrace's sin, and sends the climber on.
The hours are pictured as maidservants of the day, taking turns. The sixth has finished her shift: it is just past noon. This is Easter Monday, the travelers' second day on the mountain.
The planet Venus before dawn. Lucifer, the fallen angel carved at the start of the pavement, bears the morning star's name. This angel shows what he threw away.
It is not clear whether the angel or Dante speaks these three lines. Either way they echo the Gospel: "Many are called, but few are chosen" (Matthew 22:14).

quote: struck my forehead with his wings
note: The angel at the gate cut seven P's into Dante's forehead with his sword (Canto 9), one for each deadly sin: P for peccatum, Latin for sin. This stroke wipes away the first, the P of pride, though Dante does not know it yet.
San Miniato al Monte, on its hill across the Arno from the center of Florence. It looks down over the city. A long flight of steps climbed to it.

context: Sarcasm from an exile. The next lines recall two scandals in the city's government.

note: A bridge over the Arno, now called the Ponte alle Grazie. It was named for Rubaconte da Mandella, the Milanese governor of Florence who laid its first stone in 1237.

Two Florentine frauds of Dante's time. About 1299 two officials tore a page out of a public record book to hide a crime. And an officer of the salt tax, one of the Chiaramontesi family, removed a stave from the tub used to measure salt, so that he could give short measure and pocket the difference.

quote: Blessed are the poor in spirit
note: The first of the Beatitudes, the blessings Christ gives in the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5:3). It is sung in Latin: Beati pauperes spiritu. One Beatitude is heard at the exit of every terrace. The poor in spirit are the humble.
The first sounds of Hell were sighs, cries and wailing in the dark (Inferno 3).
Six of the seven marks are left. Pride is the root of the other sins, so with the first P gone the rest have already grown faint.
The law of the mountain: the climb is hardest at the bottom and grows easier as sin is shed (Canto 4). When all seven marks are gone, going up will be as natural as falling is for a stone.
A homely, comic simile after the solemn carvings: a man in the street who gathers from people's looks that something is stuck on his head, and feels for it with his hand.
The angel who guards the gate of Purgatory and holds Saint Peter's two keys (Canto 9).
One of Virgil's rare smiles, at the sight of Dante counting his forehead with his fingers.
